title: A single design choice determines whether machine learning models of materials make physically impossible predictions
authors: Can Polat, Mustafa Kurban, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban
abstract: Machine-learned models are replacing first-principles calculations across materials discovery, and physical symmetry is the central guarantee built into them. The debate over how much symmetry to hard-wire rather than learn has run on rotations, where a symmetry error is an approximation error. Some constraints are exact: symmetry forces certain property tensors to exactly zero, so a nonzero prediction is physically impossible rather than inaccurate. Here we show that whether a model can make such predictions is decided before training by one rarely reported design bit, whether its features carry parity labels, and derive a criterion, the parity gap, that computes from group theory alone which properties and crystals are exposed. Across matched architecture pairs differing only in that bit, evaluated on two thousand centrosymmetric crystals whose piezoelectric tensor must vanish, parity-labelled arms sit at the floating-point floor while rotation-only arms predict forbidden responses on 90-96% of crystals, six orders of magnitude apart, at no accuracy cost. Training on explicit zeros does not recover exactness, and a head on a frozen universal potential inherits its backbone's symmetry group. One reflection at random initialization verifies the label in seconds.
summary: This work demonstrates that for ML models predicting material properties, the inclusion of parity labels in the model's features is the single design element that dictates whether the model respects exact physical symmetries. Models lacking this label frequently predict physically impossible, non-zero values for properties that must vanish due to crystal symmetry.
main_problem: The paper addresses whether machine learning models designed for materials can predict physically impossible properties due to insufficient incorporation of exact symmetry constraints.
main_result: The ability to enforce exact symmetry constraints (like zero for centrosymmetric materials) is determined solely by a single design choice: whether the model's features are explicitly labeled with parity information.
method: The authors derive the 'parity gap' from group theory to quantify the difference between approximate (rotational) and exact symmetry constraints, testing this using ML models trained on materials data.
model_or_system: The system is crystalline materials, and the models are machine-learned surrogates for first-principles calculations, specifically tested on properties like the piezoelectric tensor.
key_observables: The predicted magnitude of the piezoelectric tensor, and the 'false-flag fraction' (percentage of predictions exceeding a physical threshold when the true value is zero).
important_parameters: The parity label (a binary design choice), the symmetry group ($	ext{E}(3)$ vs $	ext{SO}(3)$), and the physical threshold ($	au = 0.01 	ext{ C m}^{-2}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the validity of permutation and translation invariance, and crucially, that the parity label is an 'upstream' design choice.
figures_summary: Figures compare the predictions of parity-labelled ($	ext{O}(3)$) vs. parity-blind ($	ext{SO}(3)$) models for the piezoelectric tensor, showing a separation of six orders of magnitude, with the $	ext{SO}(3)$ model frequently predicting forbidden, non-zero responses.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical distinction between approximate and exact symmetry constraints, derives the parity gap criterion, and then empirically demonstrates this gap by comparing the performance of ML architectures that either incorporate or ignore parity labels when predicting physical tensors.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter ML, the rigorous mathematical framework for enforcing exact physical laws (like zero tensors) through structural design choices is highly relevant to building reliable quantum simulation models.
